# Case Study: Best Practice vs. Anti-Pattern

Compare the two tasks (bootstrap $B=10,000$ / Gibbs $4\text{ chains}\times20,000\text{ iter}$) across five implementations:

| Implementation | Characteristics (anti-pattern → improvement) |
|---|---|
| Naive R | `for` + `rbind`, `solve(t(X) %*% X)`, repeated `lm()` calls |
| Vectorized R | `apply`/matrix ops, `crossprod`, pre-allocation |
| Naive Rcpp | R habits carried over: `push_back`, pass-by-value, recomputing $X^{T}X$ inside the loop, `inv()` |
| Optimized Rcpp | Ch4–7 applied: pre-allocation, `const&`, Cholesky, hoisting computation out of loops, object-based Gibbs |
| Parallel Optimized Rcpp | Ch8 applied: RcppParallel, 1/2/4/8 cores |

- Metrics: wall time, peak memory, estimated energy (kWh), CO2e (table + figures)
- Verify that statistical results are identical (bootstrap CI, posterior summaries): faster but wrong is meaningless
- **Key points**
  - Where the biggest gain comes from
  - Parallelization $\neq$ always green: energy = time $\times$ power. If speedup is sublinear, adding cores can increase total energy
  - Development time vs running time: code run once vs code run ten thousand times
- Checklist — 10 questions to ask yourself before/after writing Rcpp code
